outputs.L1:
Here are two polished versions of your text. Because the original is deeply poetic and surreal, these options enhance its eloquence, cadence, and structure while preserving every piece of imagery and meaning.

### Option 1: Eloquent Literary Prose
*Best for a polished narrative, essay, or prose-poem format.*

> This persistent phase continues without variation, jazz, or compromise, allowing blue snow to grow against the windowpanes. Fumes of mohair choke my throat like cat fur; heatless flames pounce, and shadows clad in parkas gather behind my back. Turn so I may see your face; stand where I can see you, man. 
>
> Should anyone call, I will tell whoever it is that I cannot escape this night. Even the sound of saxophones fails to dry the light, the brown sweat, or the terror lurking in white doorways. Beneath multicolored covers, sleep is impossible with the phone dangling off its hook and the blaring beeps of warning: *Do not leave your house; do not stay home.* This is the central contradiction of the era in which I live. 
>
> Even fanfares and grand flourishes fail to announce a truce with our personal assailants. Without variety, blue dust, traces of blood in the floor wax, black fog, and nappy lint endure, while colorless wax trails broad tears across every window. It is as though some permanent weather has settled upon this building—as if a misplaced coal mine suffered its disaster here—and yet, I remain alive inside.

---

### Option 2: Atmospheric & Elevated Verse
*Best for retaining a modern, rhythmic, avant-garde tone while adding clarity and elegance.*

> This little phase persists unchanged—
> without variety, jazz, or compromise—
> making blue snow grow at the windows. 
> 
> Mohair fumes clog my throat like cats. 
> Flames pounce without burning; 
> shadows gather in parkas at my back.

>

> colorless wax spreads broad tears across all the windows. 
> 
> Some permanent weather happened to this building; 
> some misplaced coal mine had its disaster here,

outputs.L2:
This current period drags on without change, lacking improvisation or concession, causing azure snow to build up against the glass panes. Woolen vapors choke my throat like felines, and heatless blazes spring out without scorching anything. Behind my back, darkness dressed in heavy hooded coats congregates; swivel around so your features become visible, and position yourself directly within my view, friend. 

If a telephone call comes through, I will inform whoever is on the line that fleeing this darkness is impossible. Not even the sound of saxophones can absorb the light, the murky perspiration, or the panic haunting pale thresholds. Rest remains unattainable under vibrant blankets while the telephone dangles unhooked; its piercing warning tone issues paradoxical demands—to neither remain indoors nor depart—reflecting the contradictory nature of my era. Even ceremonial brass music cannot signal a cease-fire with the adversaries targeting us individually. 

Devoid of any alteration, there is azure powder, streaks of blood trapped in floor polish, dark mist, and woolly fluff. Clear wax streams down every windowpane like large weeping droplets. It is as if a perpetual climate took hold of this facility, or an errant subterranean mine met catastrophe right here—yet I remain breathing on the inside.
outputs.L3:
Day after day unfolds in a suffocating, repetitive loop from which there is no apparent escape. The world has shrunk into a claustrophobic nightmare where time loses its meaning, trapping the speaker in an inescapable cycle of stagnation and dread. 

The physical environment offers no respite, saturated with toxic fumes and the sharp, stomach-turning stench of deep-seated decay. The sensory overload is heavy and oppressive, evoking the agonizing terror of a subterranean catastrophe—reminiscent of a coal mine collapse where the walls press inward and oxygen becomes a forgotten luxury. 

This physical imprisonment is compounded by a psychological siege. Conflicting public directives flood the airwaves, creating a landscape of profound paranoia and paralysis. Official bulletins simultaneously command citizens to shelter in place and to evacuate immediately. Trapped between the fear of staying and the threat of leaving, the speaker is rendered entirely motionless by these irreconcilable warnings.

Even within the walls of home, peace remains unattainable. Rest is impossible, stripped away by an unyielding current of terror and endless disruptions. High-pitched emergency alarms blare at random intervals, shattering the silence, while the telephone sits unhooked off its cradle, emitting a persistent, unnatural tone that serves as a constant reminder of broken connections and impending doom.

In the end, traditional avenues of comfort offer no sanctuary. Neither the soothing cadence of music nor the execution of grand, dramatic gestures can negotiate a truce or grant relief. The personal assailants at the door remain undeterred, leaving the speaker entirely exposed to the threats closing in from all sides.
outputs.L4:
Black soot falls like dry rain, tasting of copper, old teeth, and forgotten pennies under the tongue. The air does not flow down here; it sits, a gelatinous mass of sulfur and stale carbon pressing hard against my eyelids until the dark begins to bloom in neon violet. I am in the belly of something massive and ruined, a subterranean labyrinth of wet slate, rusted girders, and decaying timber. A coal mine, perhaps, or the hollowed-out carcass of a building that collapsed into itself before I was born. The walls sweat a cold, black grease that drips with the slow, agonizing cadence of a deathwatch beetle. 

I try to step forward, but my feet are rooted in the silt. The shaft is shrinking. I can feel the granite ceiling lowering inch by agonizing inch, dripping liquid lead onto the crown of my head, yet my body refuses the command to flee. Paralysis is not a void; it is a weight, a heavy coat forged from lead and panic that wraps tight around my limbs until my bones feel brittle as dry chalk. 

Above me—or perhaps inside my ears—the sirens do not sound a warning so much as they argue with one another. A cracked loudspeaker spits a voice full of static and dead moths: *Step left into the darkness, the light will burn your retinas, inhalation is safety.* But the chalk writing scrawled across the rotting pit-props screams a different command: *DO NOT MOVE. THE AIR IS ACID. TURN BACK.* The arrows painted on the damp walls point toward each other, a carousel of conflicting exits that circle endlessly into the deep. *Breathe in,* the silence tells me. *Hold it until your lungs burst,* the echoes whisper back. Every signal is a trap; every direction is an execution.

The gas creeps in like a silver mist, smelling of burnt hair and sweet, rotting apples. My throat constricts, a tight knot of muscle rejecting the atmosphere. By every law of biology, my heart should have stopped hours ago. The yellow canary in the wire cage at my hip went stiff before the last lamp flickered out, its tiny feathers turning black and dropping away like singed paper. Yet my lungs continue their obscene, rhythmic pumping. They draw the poison in, converting it into a feverish blood-heat. I am impossibly, inexplicably alive, trapped in a biological paradox—a corpse that refuses to stop breathing the very air that killed it.

Out of the gloom, the shadows begin to detach themselves from the coal seams. They do not have monsters' faces; they have faces I know. They are the shapes of old mistakes, sharp words spoken in lit rooms years ago, the cold geometry of ancient guilt. They carry pickaxes forged from my own memories, whistling tunes I thought I had forgotten. 

They move closer, filling the narrow corridor until there is no air left between us. I wait for the final strike, the merciful cave-in that will bury us all, but it never comes. There is no collapse. There is no rescue team digging down through the rock. The building is not made of stone and iron; it is constructed from the architecture of my own terror, and the men with the pickaxes are the only inhabitants I have ever truly known. I am sealed in the deep dark with my own creators, breathing the poison of my own lingering past, wide awake in a war where the enemy sleeps in my blood and no truce will ever be declared.
outputs.L5:
We often use the words **“this little phase”** as a shield. We offer them as a gentle consolation to exhausted parents, a reassuring nod to a friend undergoing a career crisis, or a quiet whisper to ourselves when we feel hopelessly stuck. 

*“Don’t worry,”* we say, waving a hand as if dismissing a passing cloud. *“It’s just a little phase.”*

There is a profound comfort in labeling our struggles as temporary. When the baby wakes up every two hours, calling it a phase keeps insanity at bay. When a teenager retreats behind a locked bedroom door and a wall of silence, calling it a phase preserves hope. When we find ourselves in a season of creative drought, self-doubt, or quiet melancholy, telling ourselves that it is merely a phase allows us to breathe through the weight of it. It reminds us that time is moving, even when we feel frozen in place.

Yet, calling something a "little phase" is a fascinating psychological trick. It minimizes the present moment so that we can survive it. But in doing so, we sometimes overlook the subtle magic hidden within these transient chapters.

Consider how a life is built. It is not a continuous, smooth highway; it is an archipelago of distinct phases, linked together by the passage of time. The phase where you wore exclusively black and listened to angst-ridden music shaped your empathy. The phase where you lived on instant noodles in a tiny, overpriced apartment taught you resilience. The phase where you felt utterly lost in your late twenties forced you to figure out who you actually were when no one was watching.

None of those phases felt "little" while you were living them. They felt monumental. They took up the entirety of your sky.

And then, there are the phases we wish would last forever. The phase where your child still wants to hold your hand while walking to the park. The phase of a new relationship where every conversation feels like discovering a new continent. The quiet, golden summer where time seemed to slow down just for you. We rarely call these "phases" while we are in them, but in hindsight, we realize they were as fleeting as any storm.

Perhaps the secret to living well is learning to respect **this little phase**—whatever it happens to be for you right now. 

If your current phase is difficult, exhausting, or boring, take comfort in its expiration date. You will not be in this exact place forever. The storm will exhaust itself; the fog will lift. 

And if your current phase is joyful, sweet, or peaceful, hold it tightly. Don't rush through it to get to the next big milestone. 

In the end, our lives are nothing more than a mosaic of these fleeting seasons. We do not simply outgrow them; we are assembled by them. So take a deep breath, look around at where you are today, and trust the process. After all, it’s just this little phase—and it is making you who you are meant to be.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in a stream-of-consciousness style exploring themes of urban paranoia, nightmarish weather, and isolation. Use vivid, avant-garde imagery involving jazz, strange fumes, and claustrophobia.
counterfactuals.output: The sky is a bruised throat strangling on its own heavy mercury, dropping swollen purple cumulus down to the rusted fire escapes where copper vapors bloom like rotten orchids, sweet and thick with old exhaust, tasting of penny-metal and forgotten teeth. I walk inside the sound of a muted trumpet—a solitary, fractured, B-flat minor panic skittering across the slick cobblestones—and every shadow has a sharp elbow, every third-story window a dilated iris tracking the wet wool of my coat as it shrinks, tighter, tighter against my shivering ribs. Pressure, sudden pressure, the grid of the city is leaning in, brick by suffocating brick, alleyways folding themselves into tight origami pockets that pinch the air out of my throat, trapping my breath behind a rising curtain of curdled neon. Did you hear that? The sewer grate is playing bebop backwards, a frantic, improvisational hiss of hot lavender smog and screeching brass, boiling up from the subterranean gut to singe my heels, but when I turn there is no one, only the suffocating sky descending like a wet felt hat pulled down past my jaw. I try to swallow the night but it is all static and zinc, a phantom snare drum tap-tap-tapping against the inside of my teeth, whispering that the streetlights are optical lenses zooming in on the pulse in my neck. The buildings grow knees, the sidewalk buckles into a tongue, the rain begins to fall upward in jagged needles of black glass, and I am compressed, a solitary sliver of meat wedged between two concrete jaws, chewing on the dial tone of a dead landline, waiting for the weather to snap its teeth and bite through the roof of my mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a paragraph about existential dread during an inescapable night. Make it sound like surreal beat poetry without standard sentence structure.
counterfactuals.output: Clock-face bleeding onto the nightstand, dig, 3:33 AM running on a broken tape loop while the dark comes down heavy like a wet wool suit stuffed with lead and forgotten phone numbers—no dawn coming, no sunrise baby, just the long bruised indigo of the big silent screech soaking through plaster and skin—and the cosmic Nada, that cold cat, blowing a low blues note straight through the ribcage into the hollow marrow. Trapped in the zero-vault. Shadow-spiders sipping the electric hum of the fridge while the ceiling recedes into lightyears of black velvet nowhere, and you’re awake—so radically, horribly awake—riding an elevator of sheer panic plunging down through your own unblinking eyes into the endless, bottomless, inescapable jazz-abyss of the forever-night.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a surrealist text that incorporates the following elements: blue snow, saxophones, blaring phone warnings, colorless wax, and a coal mine disaster inside a building.
counterfactuals.output:
The sky inside the grand atrium had finally turned its pockets inside out, spilling **blue snow** over the mahogany banisters of the eighth floor. It fell upward first, then drifted down in heavy, cobalt tufts, settling upon the shoulders of the marble statues like bruised frost.

Below, in the copy room, the floorboards began to groan under the weight of an impossible depth. A **coal mine disaster** had broken out between the water cooler and the paper shredder. Shaft Number Four had collapsed directly into the main hallway; the drywall buckled into sheer walls of glittering anthracite, and thick, black soot filled the air, dusting the chandeliers. Blind canaries fluttered out of filing cabinets, their yellow feathers stained ash-gray, while miners with headlamps like dying stars emerged from the elevator shafts, digging frantically through the Persian rugs to shore up the collapsing ceiling of timber and ceiling tiles.

Through the gloom, the **saxophones** began to bloom. They sprouted from the brass plumbing fixtures like heavy, curlicued orchids, their golden bells pulsing with a sluggish, unwritten blues. They played without lip or finger, exhaling notes made of warm indigo smoke that curled around the blue drifts of indoor snow.

Then came the **blaring phone warnings**.

Every receiver in the building—the rotary phones buried under carbon dust, the cracked smartphones trapped in desk drawers, the red emergency box on the stairwell landing—erupted at once. The sound was not a ring, but a sharp, digital panic, a synchronized screech that split the air like sheet metal tearing. *EMERGENCY ALERT*, the illuminated screens throbbed through the black dust. *THE MOUNTAIN HAS SUNK TO THE NINTH FLOOR. DO NOT BREATHE THE VELVET.*

To escape the sound, the typists dipped their hands into the deep stone basins of **colorless wax** that bubbled silently in the corners of the room. The wax was clear as distilled water, odorless and instantly cold. They painted their ears with it, then their eyes, sealing themselves into transparent, glossy cocoons. 

Outside the windows, where the sky should have been, there was only more wallpaper. As the miners dug through the shattered linoleum toward the roof, and the saxophones wept their heavy brass ice into the blue drifts, the entire building hardened into a quiet, clear shell—listening only to the endless, muffled scream of a phone that no one was left to answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine an apartment building caught in an impossible, permanent storm where the city's warning system tells residents simultaneously "do not leave your house" and "do not stay home." Write a dark, poetic interior monologue from a resident trying to endure the night amidst bizarre hallucinations and atmospheric decay.
counterfactuals.output:
The emergency broadcast box above the dead radiator does not speak in a voice meant for lungs. It clicks, a rhythmic, metallic stutter, like a beetle trapped in a jar, before bleeding its red LED text across the dark:

*DO NOT LEAVE YOUR HOUSE.*
*DO NOT STAY HOME.*

I read it until the words lose their shapes and become black strokes floating against my retinas. Outside, the storm is not weather; it is a weight. It has been three days—or three centuries—since the sky turned the color of a wet slate shingle and stayed there, pressed so hard against the windowpane that the glass bows inward, groaning like an old ship’s hull. 

Where do you go when the sanctuary is a cage and the outside is an abyss? 

I sit on the edge of the velvet armchair, my feet pulled up, refusing to touch the rug. The carpet has begun to sweat. A dark, salty brine seeps up through the weave, smelling of dredged riverbeds and ancient, rusted copper. If I step down, I feel the floor give way beneath my heels—not breaking, but yielding, soft and pulpy like the skin of an overripe plum. The apartment building is digesting itself. 

*Do not leave.*
The hallway beyond my front door is no longer a hallway. I looked through the peephole an hour ago. The brass circle didn't show the fluorescent lights or Mrs. Gable’s doormat. It showed a vertical drop of black, swirling fog, lit from below by pale, pulsing ribbons of green static. I heard the elevator cables snapping in the shaft, one by one, playing a slow, agonizing song of tension and release. To step out would be to fall upwards into a sky that smells of ozone and dead ferns.

*Do not stay.*
The wallpaper in the dining room is peeling in long, velvet strips, revealing not drywall behind it, but wet, gray ribs of exposed lath that expand and contract. The room is breathing. Slowly, heavily, in time with my own shallow pulse. When I close my eyes, I can hear the plaster humming. Mushrooms—pale, translucent things that look like tiny, severed thumbs—have sprouted in the corner where my books are piled. They glow with a cold, sickly bioluminescence, casting long, twisting shadows that move even when I hold my breath.

I look at my hands. In the dim, red pulse of the warning box, my knuckles look like polished stone. The skin between my fingers feels stretched, thin as cellophane. 

A shadow detaches itself from the coat rack by the door. It doesn't walk; it flows across the wet rug, a smear of darkness darker than the night, taking the shape of someone I used to know—or perhaps just the memory of a posture. It stands at the edge of the hallway, leaning inward, whispering in a sound like dry leaves scraping over concrete.

*“It’s time to go,”* it says, using my mother’s voice, but pitched an octave too low, dragged through silver dust. 
*“It’s time to settle in,”* it says, using my own voice, coming from the back of my closet.

I cover my ears, but the storm is inside the room now. The rain isn't falling from above; it’s rising from the baseboards, fine mist drifting upward toward the ceiling, defying gravity, pooling in trembling, upside-down puddles around the light fixture. A single drop detaches and falls *up*, striking the glass shade with a soft *ping*.

The dual mandate flashes again. Red. Black. Red. Black.
*SEEK COVER. EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY.*

A cruel, bureaucratic joke written by an panicked city that no longer exists, broadcast by an automated heart that doesn't know the ribs have collapsed around it. They locked us in the paradox. To obey one is to violate the other. So we are caught in the margin—the thin, papery seam between the inside and the outside, where time curdles and the spatial logic of a four-walled room dissolves into mist.

I stand up. The rug yields, swallowing my socks in icy, black brine. 

I walk toward the door. I walk toward the window. I do neither. I stand precisely in the center of the living room, right where the ceiling is bowing lowest, right where the drywall is weeping its white dust into my hair. 

I open my mouth to scream, but what comes out is only the sound of the gale—a low, resonant whistle through a hollow bone. I am not leaving. I am not staying. I am becoming the weather. I am becoming the dark, sweet rot of the fifth floor, waiting for the ceiling to finally meet the floor and press me into a sliver of forgotten time.

The LED blinks. 
*DO NOT...*
*DO NOT...*

The rest of the words melt into the dark, and at last, the rain begins to sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Channel a noir poet writing a claustrophobic, jazz-drenched nightmare about being stuck indoors while reality unravels outside the window.
counterfactuals.output:
The four walls are a bad contract, 
signed in nicotine, damp plaster, and rust.
The ceiling hangs low as a heavyweight’s jaw,
dripping staccato sweat onto the worn linoleum.
Down the airshaft, a muted trumpet bleeds a flat-five chord—
no player attached, just the brass ghost of a dead midnight
crying out for a hit it’s never gonna get.

I squeeze between the armchair and the creeping shadow.
The room is four inches narrower than it was at ten o'clock.
It smells of cheap rye, stale tobacco, and the cold, 
metallic tang of a panic that won't show its badge.

I part the Venetian blinds with two yellowed fingers.

Outside, the city is losing its mind in B-flat.
The asphalt has gone soft, slick as grease, 
refuse-wet and reflecting a moon that split in two an hour ago.
The neon sign for *LOU’S LOUNGE* screams a filthy, neon pink,
then spills off the brickwork, melting into the gutter
like fresh lipstick on a hot corpse.

Look at the streetlights—
they’re bending like drunk alley cats,
folding their steel spines, weeping sparks into the fog.
A Buick glides past the curb: no driver, no engine, 
just a hollow shell of chrome floating through a sky 
the color of a bruised liver. 
The sky doesn't hold clouds anymore; 
it holds tears in the canvas. 
I can see the black void behind the stars, 
grinding its teeth.

Listen. You hear that ride cymbal?
*Ch-ch-ch-shhh.*
That ain't a wire brush on drumhead, kid.
That’s the glass in the pane shivering.
That’s the horizon snapping like an old banjo string.
Time is dropping its beats. The syncopation is rotten.
We’re playing a nightmare in thirteen-eight,
and the bandleader just walked out the door into nothing at all.

I back away from the window, but the room won't let me breathe.
The wallpaper’s weeping dark ink, the roses curling into ash.
The floorboards groan, pulling back their nails,
showing me the basement beneath the building—
a bottomless drop of double-bass rumbling and black velvet.

I pour two fingers of poison I can’t afford.
The ice cube melted yesterday, 
but the glass is cold enough to burn skin.

Out there, the world is unspooling off its reel,
bubbling, popping, burning brown under a hot projector bulb.
The skyscrapers are tilting, kissing in the dark, 
dissolving into static and smoke.

The trumpet takes one last solo outside—
a high, terrified screech that shatters the top floor of the bank.
Then, silence. The bad kind. The kind that comes with a drawn snub-nosed.

I pull the blinds shut. 
I sit back down in the dark.
I strike a match against the arm of the chair,
watch the flame dance its little, frantic jig,
and wait for the walls to finally meet in the middle.

Keep that bassline walking, babe.
It’s the only thing keeping us on the floor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
